title: Fili Village and the Site of the Military Council
shortDescription: The historic area of the former village of Fili, where the Russian army held its Military Council on 1 (13) September 1812.
content: In the early nineteenth century, Fili was a small village in the Naryshkin family's Fili-Kuntsevo estate, about two versts west of what was then Moscow.

On 1 (13) September 1812, the Russian army held a Military Council at Fili in the hut of the peasant Mikhail Frolov. After the Battle of Borodino, the commanders debated whether to fight another general battle outside Moscow; Mikhail Kutuzov decided to abandon the city without another battle and preserve the army.

After Napoleon's army entered Moscow, the war directly affected Fili as well. According to the Battle of Borodino Panorama Museum, a military unit and a Württemberg hospital were later stationed here.

The historic village no longer exists as a separate settlement and has long since become part of Moscow's built-up area. The point on the modern map therefore marks the area of historic Fili, rather than the village's exact boundaries or a single established location for the events of 1812.
locationNote: The marker indicates the general area of the historic site; the village occupied a larger territory.
historicalNote: The present Kutuzov Hut is an 1887 reconstruction.

title: Kutuzov Hut
shortDescription: An 1887 museum building on the site of the hut where the Military Council was held.
content: The Military Council of 1 (13) September 1812 took place not in the present museum building, but in the hut of the peasant Mikhail Frolov. This was the place where Mikhail Kutuzov decided to abandon Moscow without another general battle.

The original hut was preserved as a memorial site, but it was almost completely destroyed by fire in 1868. In 1883, the site of the former hut was marked by a milepost erected on the initiative of, and with funds from, officers of the Grenadier Corps.

In 1887, a new wooden building designed by the architect D. M. Strukov was erected on the site of the earlier hut. It housed a museum devoted to the events of 1812. Today's Kutuzov Hut is therefore a historical reconstruction and museum, not the original building in which the Military Council met.

Over time, an entire memorial complex developed around the hut. The Chapel of the Archangel Michael and other memorials appeared nearby, followed in the twentieth century by the Battle of Borodino Panorama Museum and the monument to Kutuzov.
historicalNote: The existing building is not the original hut of 1812.

title: Church of the Intercession at Fili
shortDescription: A surviving late-seventeenth-century church that suffered during the presence of French troops.
content: The Church of the Intercession at Fili was built long before the Patriotic War of 1812 and was already standing here during the war. Unlike many sites in this project, it is a surviving building from the historic area, rather than a later reconstruction or memorial.

Part of the village of Fili burned during the presence of enemy troops. The state historical and cultural assessment of the Fili-Kuntsevo area reports that French soldiers kept horses inside the Church of the Intercession.

The church therefore matters to the map for more than its architectural value. It remains one of the few physical witnesses to the area through which the war passed in 1812, helping visitors relate today's urban landscape to that of the early nineteenth century.

title: Kuntsevo Estate
shortDescription: The historic site of the Naryshkin estate, whose main house burned in 1812.
content: Kuntsevo formed part of the Naryshkin family's Fili-Kuntsevo estate west of Moscow. The estate grounds existed before the Patriotic War of 1812 and formed part of the western suburban landscape.

According to the state historical and cultural assessment, the Kuntsevo house burned during the presence of enemy troops. It had been restored by 1818; the assessment considers it more likely that the main house was built anew on its former site.

In 1818, King Frederick William III of Prussia and Emperor Alexander I stopped at Kuntsevo before entering Moscow. The estate's postwar history became a story of recovery rather than the destruction of 1812.

The present main house therefore cannot be described as an unchanged building that directly 'survived Napoleon.' What matters to this project is the historic estate site, the fire of 1812 and the subsequent rebuilding.
historicalNote: The present main house should not be described as a house that “survived Napoleon.”

title: Poklonnaya Hill
shortDescription: A historic area on the western approach to Moscow associated with the advance of Napoleon’s army.
content: Poklonnaya Hill stood on the western approach to Moscow, beside the road along which the Grande Armée advanced towards the city. Tradition associates this area with one of the best-known stories of Moscow in 1812: Napoleon waiting for representatives of the city before entering it.

The account of Napoleon waiting here for a delegation and the 'keys to Moscow' became firmly established in historical memory and culture. It should not, however, be treated as an exact geographical reconstruction with a reliably established modern location.

Over two centuries, the terrain and built environment of Poklonnaya Hill have changed considerably. The project's marker therefore indicates a historic area on the western approach to Moscow, not a point where Napoleon's precise position can be stated with confidence.

The area around Poklonnaya Hill later became a place of remembrance for wars. The Triumphal Gates were recreated nearby in the twentieth century, giving the history of Moscow's western entrance a new memorial setting.
locationNote: The coordinate marks the modern historic area.
historicalNote: The story of the “keys to Moscow” should be presented as a historical tradition.

title: Dorogomilovskaya Gate
shortDescription: A lost gate on the western boundary of old Moscow.
content: The Dorogomilovskaya Gate stood by the Kamer-Kollezhsky Val on the western boundary of old Moscow. The Mozhaisk route, one of the main roads linking the city with its western outskirts, passed through it.

In 1812, Dorogomilovo lay directly on the route taken by Napoleon's army as it entered Moscow from the west. The history of the gate connects the approach through Poklonnaya Hill and Dorogomilovo with the city's former boundary.
The Dorogomilovo area suffered badly during the Moscow fire, and its layout and buildings changed over the following decades. The historic gate itself has not survived.
The modern square and road network do not reproduce the gate's early-nineteenth-century position exactly. The map marker should be read as an approximate location for a lost historic site.
locationNote: The modern square does not fully coincide with the location of the historic gate.

title: Dorogomilovskoye Cemetery and Mass Grave
shortDescription: A lost cemetery where Russian soldiers who died of wounds after Borodino were buried.
content: Dorogomilovskoye Cemetery was established outside the city boundary in the eighteenth century. After the Battle of Borodino, it became one of Moscow's places of remembrance for the war: Russian soldiers who died of their wounds were buried here.

Several hundred participants in the Battle of Borodino were buried near the cemetery church. One chapel in the stone church built in 1839–1844 was dedicated to the memory of Russian soldiers who died of wounds after Borodino.

In 1849, the Prokhorov factory owners funded a memorial over the mass grave in the form of a brick tent-roofed chapel with commemorative inscriptions. The burial site thus became both a cemetery and one of Moscow's early memorials to the war of 1812.
The cemetery was abolished in the twentieth century and is now a lost historic site. The map coordinate marks the approximate area of the former cemetery, not a surviving grave.
locationNote: The marker indicates the approximate centre of a large historic area.

title: Obelisk in Memory of the Soldiers of the Battle of Borodino
shortDescription: A granite obelisk erected in 1940, originally placed over a mass grave at Dorogomilovskoye Cemetery and later moved to the Kutuzov Hut.
content: The story of the present obelisk begins with a mass grave at Dorogomilovskoye Cemetery, where several hundred Russian soldiers who died of wounds after the Battle of Borodino were buried. In 1849, the Prokhorov family funded a memorial over the grave in the form of a brick tent-roofed chapel.
By 1940, the old memorial had deteriorated and was replaced by a new granite obelisk. The 1849 memorial and the granite obelisk that stands today are therefore not the same physical object.

The granite obelisk was later moved to the Kutuzov Hut, where it stands today. Official sources give different dates for the move: the museum chronology gives 1953, while another official historical account gives 1948.
The obelisk links two separate places of remembrance: the lost Dorogomilovskoye Cemetery and the present memorial complex at Fili.
historicalNote: The present granite obelisk was created in 1940 to replace the deteriorated 1849 memorial; they are not the same physical object.

title: Memorial Milepost at Fili
shortDescription: An 1883 memorial marking the site of the hut where the Military Council was held.
content: Although the original Military Council hut was destroyed by fire in 1868, its site continued to be regarded as historic. In 1883, it was marked by a memorial proposed and funded by the Society of Officers of the Grenadier Corps.
The museum chronology describes the marker as a milepost from the Smolensk Road that was given the shape of an obelisk. It predates the present Kutuzov Hut, reconstructed in 1887.

The milepost became one of the first elements of the future memorial complex at Fili. It shows that the site began to be preserved and interpreted long before the twentieth century: already in the second half of the nineteenth century, a place of remembrance for the Military Council of 1812 was deliberately taking shape here.

title: Chapel of the Archangel Michael
shortDescription: A memorial chapel by the Kutuzov Hut, consecrated in 1912.
content: The Chapel of the Archangel Michael appeared beside the Kutuzov Hut a century after the events of 1812. It belongs not to the area's wartime buildings, but to the later memorial landscape that developed around the site of the Military Council.

The chapel was built and consecrated in the centenary year of 1912, when Moscow marked the hundredth anniversary of the Patriotic War of 1812. Franz Roubaud's Borodino panorama also opened in the city during that anniversary year.
Together with the Kutuzov Hut, the milepost and other memorials, the chapel shows how Fili gradually changed from the site of one historic event into an entire memorial complex.
address: Kutuzovsky Prospekt, by the Kutuzov Hut

title: Battle of Borodino Panorama Museum
shortDescription: Moscow’s principal museum devoted to the War of 1812; its present building opened in 1962.
content: The Battle of Borodino Panorama Museum on Kutuzovsky Prospekt opened on 18 October 1962 for the 150th anniversary of the Patriotic War of 1812. Its opening marked a new stage in the development of the memorial complex near the historic village of Fili.

The museum's central exhibit is much older than its building. Franz Roubaud created the Borodino panorama for the battle's centenary in 1912; it was first shown in a purpose-built pavilion on Chistoprudny Boulevard.

After the exhibition closed in 1918, the canvas was not displayed for decades. The panorama was restored for the 1962 anniversary and installed in the new building on Kutuzovsky Prospekt, where it gained a permanent museum setting.

Two distinct layers of remembrance thus came together in one place: the historic geography of Fili in 1812 and the twentieth-century museum culture created to preserve and explain the memory of the war.

title: Monument to Mikhail Kutuzov and the Participants in the War of 1812
shortDescription: A 1973 monument beside the Panorama Museum.
content: The monument to Mikhail Kutuzov beside the Battle of Borodino Panorama Museum was unveiled in 1973. Its central equestrian figure of the commander was created by the sculptor N. V. Tomsky; the monument became one of the later additions to the memorial complex on Kutuzovsky Prospekt.

Kutuzov is shown on horseback, surrounded by a multi-figure composition of people who took part in the war. It brings together military commanders, soldiers and partisans, so the monument honours more than the commander-in-chief alone.

Its position in front of the museum connects Kutuzov's image to the wider story of the war of 1812. It is a twentieth-century memorial, not a historic object from the time of the war, and it continued the development of Fili as a place of remembrance.

title: Triumphal Arch
shortDescription: A monument to Russia’s victory in the War of 1812, reconstructed on Kutuzovsky Prospekt.
content: Moscow's Triumphal Gates were conceived as a monument to Russia's victory in the war against Napoleon. The stone arch designed by Osip Bove was built in 1829–1834 at the Tverskaya Gate and ceremonially opened in 1834.

The original gates did not stand on the present-day Kutuzovsky Prospekt. They were dismantled during the square's reconstruction in 1936, after measurements had been taken and part of the sculptural decoration preserved.

The Triumphal Gates were recreated in 1966–1968 at a new location on Kutuzovsky Prospekt near Poklonnaya Hill. The reconstruction drew on measurements of the former monument and a surviving original model; the former guardhouses were not recreated.

The present arch is therefore a monument to the memory of the victory of 1812, not a structure that stood here during the war. Its relocation to western Moscow in the twentieth century placed it in the same memorial landscape as the Panorama Museum and the monument to Kutuzov.
